Agreement No. CE 4/2024 (HY)
Northern Metropolis Highway
– Investigation
Environmental Impact Assessment Report – San Tin Section
Conclusion of EIA Study
15.1.1.1 This EIA Report has provided an assessment of the potential environmental
impacts associated with the construction and operation of the Project, based on the
engineering design information available during the course of EIA study.
15.1.1.2 The assessment has been conducted, in accordance with the Study Brief No. ESB-
373/2025 under the EIAO and the EIAO-TM, covering the following environmental
issues:
• Air Quality Impact;
• Noise Impact;
• Water Quality Impact;
• Waste Management Implications;
• Land Contamination;
• Ecological Impact (Terrestrial and Aquatic);
• Fisheries Impact;
• Landscape and Visual Impact;
• Cultural Heritage; and
• Hazard to Life.
15.1.1.3 The findings of this EIA study have determined the likely nature and extent of
environmental impacts predicted to arise from the construction and operation of the
Project. During the EIA process, environmental control measures have been
identified and incorporated into the planning and design of the Project, to achieve
compliance with environmental legislation and standards during both the
construction and operational phases. The Implementation Schedule listing the
recommended mitigation measures is presented in the stand-alone Environmental
Monitoring & Audit Manual.
15.1.1.4 The various sections of this EIA Report have presented the measures to minimise
the potential environmental impacts associated with the Project throughout the
construction and operational phases. The key measures to minimise the
environmental impacts are summarized in Section 14.
15.1.1.5 With the implementation of the mitigation measures, the Project would be
environmentally acceptable with no unacceptable residual impacts on the
environmentally sensitive receivers and resources. Table 15.1 below summarises
the key environmental outcomes and benefits that have accrued from the
environmental considerations and analysis during the EIA process and the
implementation of environmental control measures of the Project. Appendix 15.1
presents the summary of key assessment assumptions, limitation of assessment
methodologies, while Appendix 15.2 presents the summary of environmental
impacts.
15.1.1.6 An Environmental Monitoring and Audit (EM&A) programme has been developed
to ascertain and verify the assumptions implicit to, and accuracy of, EIA study
predictions. EM&A requirements have been recommended, where necessary, to
check on project compliance of environmental legislation and standards. These are
presented in a separate stand-alone EM&A Manual.

Environmental / Social
Benefits of the Project
and Environmentally
Friendly design
• Avoidance of direct impact to ecologically sensitive areas
- The recommended alignment and its works footprint
have been thoroughly considered and evaluated from
alternative alignment options proposed in previous stage
studies (Section 2.6 of Chapter 2 refers). This process
has resulted in the recommended alignment option, which
aims to avoid potential both direct and indirect impacts on
recognised sites of conservation importance and other
ecologically sensitive areas, such as the Lam Tsuen
Country Park (LTCP), the proposed Nam Sang Wai
Wetland Conservation Park and natural watercourses at
Ngau Tam Mei. The locations of piers are also carefully
designed to avoid direct encroachment into natural
watercourses.
• Wetland Habitat Enhancement through Integration and
Expansion – Under the original alignment, an
interchange, I/C-03, (with associated site office and
ancillary facilities) was proposed to the west of Ngau Tam
Mei Water Treatment Works (NTMWTW), where
scattered and fragmented wetland habitats are currently
found. Compared to the original alignment, the
recommended alignment has been refined, with the
Interchange I/C-03 relocated to the south of Ngau Tam
Mei New Development Area (NTM NDA). The viaduct
level has also been raised as much as practicable to
provide greater clearance allowing natural sunlight to
reach the habitats underneath the viaduct structures. The
relocation of Interchange I/C-03 to the south of NTM NDA
will also provide an opportunity to integrate and expand
the wetland habitats to the west of NTMWTW.
Furthermore, the mainline will be constructed as an
elevated viaduct with a limited number of piers, spanning
over the wetland habitats to reduce direct ecological
impact to this wetland habitats. Taking advantage of the
Project implementation, the area will not only be
reinstated, but the existing fragmented wetland habitats
will also be integrated and enhanced into a connected
wetland habitat. The total wetland area will increase from
approximately 3 hectares of fragmented ponds to more
than 5 hectares of integrated wetland habitats through the
incorporation of adjacent village / orchard land. With
improved design and management, the enhanced
wetland habitat will support higher biodiversity, greater
ecological value and increased carrying capacity. It will
also offer a suitable foraging environment for various
relevant species, including waterbirds.
• Allowing Wildlife Movement by Adopting Intermittent
At‑grade and Viaduct Design – A section of the alignment
runs adjacent to the woodland habitat at the edge of the
Lam Tsuen Country Park (LTCP) near Long Ha. The
alignment profile has been raised as far as practicable,
taking into account site constraints such as CLP cables,
pylons and traffic design requirements. The design has
been optimised to avoid encroachment into LTCP while

For the at-grade sections, retaining wall on the slope

• Viaduct Level Arrangement and Carriageway Separation
for Enhancing Sunlight Penetration and Ecological
Benefits – The Project includes slip roads crossing the
Kam Tin River, where the viaduct level has been adjusted
to provide headroom of about 10~15m and minimise
shading effects on the water body and associated
habitats. In the vicinity of NTMWTW, to accommodate the
required clearance from the existing CLP cable, the
headroom beneath the viaduct is approximately 10m for
the northbound and ranges from 5m to 10m for the
southbound. The dual carriageways are separated before
entering the tunnel portal. The resulting gap between the
carriageways enables natural sunlight to reach the
ground below and is not expected to cause adverse
ecological impacts. Furthermore, the positioning of piers
have been refined to avoid encroachment into natural
watercourses. This approach helps to minimize potential
water quality and ecological impact.
• Adoption of non-dredged method for construction works
at Kam Tin River - The significance of ecological value of
Kam Tin River is well recognised. Given the large span of
the viaduct crossing Kam Tin River, the pile /pier support
within the river is inevitable. The construction of viaduct
pier/ pile will adopt the non-dredging method. For
example, if bored pile construction is adopted, steel
casing could be adopted to isolate the surrounding
riverbed. The material within the steel casing will be
excavated within the casing for placing reinforcement and
concrete of the pile. This minimises the disturbance to the
river.
• Synergistic Woodland Enhancement near She Leng – A
woodland compensation site of approximately 17 ha is
proposed near She Leng, which is currently characterised
by grassland or shrubland of low or low to moderate
ecological value. The site is also adjacent to proposed
woodland compensation areas under other projects,
including Lok Ma Chau Loop, San Tin Technopole (STT)
and Development of the Loop – Eastern Connection
Road (ECR). Woodland compensation at this location will
integrate the overall compensatory woodland area and
improve habitat quality and ecological connectivity with
adjacent woodland habitats.
• Minimisation of slope cutting through adoption of elevated
alignment – Given the hilly terrain to the south of NTM
NDA, the road alignment has been elevated. This
adjustment not only minimises the scale of site formation
works, but also takes into account other constraints, such
as the clearance requirement for CLP power cables.

clearance between the structure and the habitats so as to

• Minimisation of slope cutting through soft ground
tunnelling at portals – When the alignment passes
through Ngau Tam Shan and Hadden Hill, soft ground
tunnelling has been adopted at portals. Specifically,
before the tunnel excavation reaches bedrock, soft soil
stratum will be improved with injection grouting around
the tunnel profile. Temporary support such as pipe roofing
and steel lattice girder/rib will be installed during the
tunnel excavation by mechanical method. With the
adoption of soft ground tunnelling, the extent of site
formation is significantly reduced, which helps retain a
larger area of natural terrain and minimise the generation
of construction and demolition (C&D) materials.
• Minimisation of slope cutting through construction of
retaining walls and soil nailing – For sections where
extensive cut slopes would otherwise be required,
retaining walls / soil nails or combination of both may be
proposed. This measure aims to reduce the extent of
slope excavation, allow for steeper slope gradients, and
thereby minimise the project’s environmental footprint, as
well as acting as a barrier to prevent wildlife roadkill.
• Avoidance of direct impacts on Sites of Archaeological
Interest (SAI) – Avoid any excavation works which will
cause potential disturbance to the soil matrix within the
boundary of Ngau Tam Mei SAI to avoid potential direct
impacts on the SAI.
• Adopt Drill and Blast (D&B) method for tunnel
construction – Adopt D&B method over TBM (Tunnel
Boring Machine) method for tunnel construction to
minimize the generation of construction & demolition
(C&D) materials as much as practicable.
• Diverting the existing traffic flow between northeast and
northwest of the New Territories, lowering vehicular
emissions from idling or congested traffic and shortening
travel times and results in further reducing fuel
consumption, alleviating potential air quality and noise
impact during operation phase.

emissions from construction vehicles. Construction

assessment area would also pose cumulative air quality
impact. With the implementation of mitigation measures

Operation Phase
• Cumulative air quality impacts were assessed by
considering the Project-induced emissions, all relevant
emission sources within the 500 m assessment area,
such as vehicular emission from open roads, tunnel
portals and facilities with vehicular emissions (existing
and planned public transport interchanges, bus and
minibus Termini, heavy goods vehicle and coach parking
sites), industrial emissions, and background

results concluded that the cumulative NO2, RSP, and
FSP concentrations at all existing and planned ASRs
would comply with the prevailing AQOs. Thus, no
adverse air quality impact on the existing and planned
ASRs would be anticipated.
Noise Impact Construction Noise
• Assessment on potential construction noise impact
arising from the Project has been conducted
qualitatively. The assessment results indicate that with
the implementation of appropriate mitigation measures,
no adverse construction noise impact would be
anticipated.
Road Traffic Noise
• While for the road traffic noise, the assessment results
indicate that the predicted road traffic noise levels at
some of the representative Noise Sensitive Receiver
(NSRs) would exceed the noise criteria under the
unmitigated scenario. Direct noise mitigation measures
have been considered to alleviate the potential traffic
noise impact. With implementation of the recommended
noise mitigation measures of Low Noise Road Surfacing
and reflective and absorptive vertical and cantilevered
type noise barrier and the provision of at-receiver
mitigation measures, such as acoustic
windows/balconies, the noise levels at all NSRs within
the assessment area would comply with the traffic noise
criteria stipulated in Clause 4.7.6 of EIAO GN No.
12/2023. As such, adverse road traffic noise impact due
to the Project is not anticipated.

Water Quality Impact • Construction of pier and viaduct structures across Kam
Tin River would require installation of cofferdam and/or
watertight pile casing to enclose the associated
construction works. Cofferdam and watertight pile casing
should be constructed to isolate the construction activities
from the river water. Cofferdam and watertight pile casing
should be designed by the Contractor which fulfil the
requirements in DSD Technical Circular No. 1/2017
"Temporary Flow Diversions and Temporary Works
Affecting Capacity in Stormwater System". Water pumps
should be used to collect any construction site runoff and
ingress/seepage water within the cofferdam and
watertight pile casing to the on-site wastewater treatment
facilities for treatment to satisfactory levels before
discharge. Silt curtain should be deployed to completely
enclose the cofferdam and watertight pile casing prior to
conduct construction works in Kam Tin River, and
installation and removal of cofferdam and/or watertight
pile casing.
• Pier construction at Kam Tin River should be conducted
by phases to avoid adverse water flow impact due to flow
blockage increase during the interim construction stages.
• Water quality impacts from land-based construction
would be controlled by implementing the recommended
mitigation measures and good site practices. Water
quality monitoring and regular site inspections would be
carried out routinely to minimise water quality impacts
upon the nearby inland waters. An Emergency Response
Plan is recommended to minimise the potential water
quality impact from construction site discharges under
failure of treatment facilities during emergency situations
or inclement weather.
• Potential water quality impacts during operation phase
were related to the non-point source surface runoff
generated from the additional paved areas, change in
flow regime due to the presence of bridge piers in Kam
Tin River, as well as sewage effluent generated from the
new administration building. Provided that the
recommended mitigation measures for the drainage
system are properly implemented and the sewage
generated from the new administration building to be
properly collected, treated and disposed, the associated
water quality impacts were expected to be minimal and
acceptable. No significant change in flow regime and
water quality in Kam Tin River was expected and
therefore, no adverse water flow and water quality
impacts on Kam Tin River was expected.
March 2026

Environmental Issue Description
Waste Management
Implications
Construction Phase
• C&D materials, excavated sediments, chemical waste
and general refuse would be generated during the
construction phase. Provided that these wastes are
handled, transported and disposed of according to the
recommended good site practices and measures, no
adverse environmental impacts (including potential
hazard, air and odour emissions, noise and wastewater
discharges) would be anticipated during the construction
phase.
Operation Phase
• General refuse and chemical waste would be generated
during the operation phase. With the implementation of
management control practices, no adverse
environmental impact would be anticipated.
Land Contamination • Site appraisals, in the form of desktop review and site
walkovers, had been carried out between September
2025 and January 2026 to identify the past and current
potentially contaminating land uses within the Project
Site. Based on the site appraisal, 30 potentially
contaminated sites, 15 sites suspected to be used for
industrial purposes were identified within the Project Site.
• Further land contamination assessments, including
further site appraisal and submission of CAP(s), should
be conducted for the whole Project Site at a later stage of
the Project when site access is available to confirm the
existing land uses / activities, identify the presence of any
potential contamination sources, and address any new
contamination issues. The associated SI works and any
necessary remediation action are recommended to be
carried out after operation of concerned site(s) has
ceased but prior to the commencement of construction
works. The recommended further assessment and
remediation works, including the submission of CAP(s),
CAR(s)/RAP(s) and RR(s) would follow the relevant
Guidance Manual, Guidance Note and Practice Guide.
• With reference to previous studies, natural occurrences
of elevated level of arsenic exist over broad areas of the
northern New Territories. A separate arsenic assessment
and remediation plan should be prepared, in consultation
with EPD, and submitted to EPD for endorsement prior to
the commencement of construction works.
• With the implementation of the recommended further
works for the Project, any soil/groundwater contamination
would be identified and properly remediated prior to the
construction works. No insurmountable land
contamination impacts to the Project are therefore
anticipated.
Ecology • The potential ecological impacts arising from the
construction works of the Project would include habitat
loss, disturbance to terrestrial habitats and associated
wildlife, potential obstruction of flight paths, mortality risks
to species of conservation importance and other indirect
impacts on sites of conservation importance, natural
habitats and associated wildlife in the vicinity. With the

Fisheries • The occupation or suspension of fisheries operation is of
negligible significance to local aquaculture production.
With the implementation of good site practices specified
in the EIA, no adverse fisheries impacts is anticipated.
Landscape and Visual • Among the approx. 67,500 nos. of existing trees within
the 100m assessment area, it is estimated that there are
9,050 nos. of trees (excluding all Leucaena leucocephala
of which removal would not require a TPRP) would be
affected.
• Under this Project, the existing landscape resources,
including vegetation, marsh or wetland and fishpond
would be affected in multiple scale subject to the
proposed works. Vegetation found within the LRs and
LCAs would either be temporarily or permanently loss.
After the completion of works, landscape mitigation
measures such as tree compensation where space is
available, reinstatement of affected landscaping area or
fishpond in like for like basis and provision of buffer
screen planting would be implemented. With the
implementation of these mitigation measures, it is
considered that residual impacts of the LRs and LCAs
would be reduced to Negligible to Slight in the operational
phase.
• In terms of the visual impact, considering the connecting
alignment to the existing infrastructures and structural
mass of proposed road works, the visual impact to the
identified key public viewers would be ranging from
Negligible to Moderate.
• Considering the scale and nature of the Project, it would
inevitably result in certain levels of residual landscape
impacts and visual impacts in relation to the loss of
hillside vegetation from hilltop and from ground level.
Nevertheless, the residual landscape impacts are
localized and limited to the project extent only without
affecting existing community, while the visual impacts are
confined within the visual envelope either involving few to
medium numbers of public viewers along hiking trail and
paths. With the implementation of the proposed
landscape and visual mitigation measures, the overall
landscape residual impacts would be from Negligible to
Moderate during construction phase, and Negligible to
Slight in operational phase, and the overall visual impacts
would be from Negligible to Moderate in operational
phase. With full implementation of the recommended
mitigation measures, unacceptable adverse residual
landscape impacts and visual impacts are not expected.
Cultural Heritage • No declared monument, proposed monument, graded
historic building, new item for grading assessment and
Government historic site identified by the Antiquities and
Monuments Office (AMO) is located within the Project
